chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Numbers That Drive Value

lessons.title: Growth, Margins and Capital Efficiency: The Three Levers of Value

children.text: In the year ended March 2025, Avenue Supermarts, which runs DMart, reported revenue of about ₹59,358 crore. Hindustan Unilever reported about ₹64,138 crore. Two large Indian companies, roughly the same size on the top line. Their profits were not close at all, and neither were the amounts of capital each needed to earn them. That is the whole subject of this lesson.

body.text: Three levers move the value of any business: how fast it grows, how much of each rupee of sales it keeps, and how much capital it must tie up to earn that rupee. Growth only creates value when the return on the capital invested beats the cost of that capital. Otherwise growth just destroys money faster.

children.text: Lever One: Margins, or What You Keep

body.caption: The three margins managers are asked about

cells: (Revenue - direct cost of goods or services) ÷ Revenue
Pricing power and how much room is left to cover everything else
How efficiently the operation converts sales into operating cash earnings
What finally reaches shareholders after depreciation, interest and tax

children.text: Now put the two real companies side by side for FY25.

body.caption: Same revenue scale, very different economics (FY25)

body.text: HUL keeps about 3.3 times as much of every rupee of sales as DMart does. That does not make DMart the weaker business. A retailer sells other companies' brands at thin margins and makes its money on volume and speed. A branded goods company sells its own brands at fat margins and spends heavily to keep them wanted. Judge a margin only against the margins of the same kind of business.

children.text: Margins also move for a reason that has nothing to do with pricing.
Operating leverage
means a business with heavy fixed costs sees profits swing far more than sales.

markDefs.definition: The effect of fixed costs on profits. When fixed costs stay flat as revenue grows, profits rise faster than revenue. The same effect works brutally in reverse when revenue falls.

body.title: Operating leverage in action
body.prompt: A company has revenue of ₹100 crore, variable costs of ₹60 crore and fixed costs of ₹30 crore, giving EBITDA of ₹10 crore. Revenue rises 20% to ₹120 crore. Variable costs rise in proportion, fixed costs do not move at all. By what percentage does EBITDA rise?
body.explanation: Variable costs go to ₹72 crore, fixed costs stay at ₹30 crore, so EBITDA becomes ₹120 crore - ₹72 crore - ₹30 crore = ₹18 crore. That is an 80% jump from ₹10 crore on a 20% rise in revenue. Now run it downwards: a 20% fall in revenue would take EBITDA to ₹2 crore. High fixed costs cut both ways, which is why cinema chains, hotels and airlines swing so violently.

children.text: Lever Two: Capital Efficiency, or What You Tie Up
Two businesses can earn the same operating profit while using wildly different amounts of capital.
Return on capital employed
measures how hard that money is working.

markDefs.definition: Operating profit divided by the capital employed in the business, usually equity plus debt less surplus cash. It measures how hard the invested money works.

body.caption: Capital employed is broadly equity plus debt, less surplus cash

children.text: Take two fictional companies. Both earn EBIT of ₹20 crore. Sahyadri Services needs ₹100 crore of capital to do it and earns 20%. Konkan Ceramics needs ₹200 crore of plant and working capital and earns 10%. If capital costs both of them 12%, one is creating value and the other is quietly destroying it, at identical operating profit.

stats.label: Sahyadri Services
stats.context: EBIT ₹20 crore on ₹100 crore of capital

stats.label: Konkan Ceramics
stats.context: EBIT ₹20 crore on ₹200 crore of capital

children.text: A large part of capital employed in Indian businesses is not plant at all. It is working capital: stock sitting in a warehouse and money owed by customers.

body.caption: The number of days cash stays locked in the business before it comes back

body.title: Count the days
body.prompt: An auto components supplier holds 60 days of inventory, gives its customers 45 days to pay, and takes 30 days of credit from its own suppliers. What is its cash conversion cycle, in days?
body.explanation: 60 + 45 - 30 = 75 days. Every rupee of sales is funded for 75 days before it returns. Grow sales 40% and the working capital requirement grows with it, which is why fast growing suppliers so often need a loan even while reporting profits.

body.title: Why the same growth costs two businesses different amounts

columns.label: Cash-rich model, as in organised retail
points: Customers pay at the till, so receivable days are close to zero
Suppliers are paid after an agreed credit period
Growth can partly fund itself through supplier credit
Thin margins are survivable because capital turns over quickly

columns.label: Capital-hungry model, as in industrial supply
points: Large corporate customers pay in 60 to 90 days
Inventory must be held to meet delivery schedules
Every rupee of extra sales needs extra working capital first
Fat margins can still leave the company short of cash

children.text: Lever Three: Growth, and When It Destroys Value
Growth is the lever everyone reaches for first and understands last. Growth requires reinvestment, and how much you must reinvest depends on the return you earn on capital.

body.caption: The share of after-tax operating profit that must go back into the business to sustain growth rate g

children.text: Two companies both want to grow 15% a year. One earns 25% on invested capital, the other earns 8%.

cells: Share of profit that must be reinvested
40% of profit is left over for shareholders
Profits are not enough. The company must raise debt or equity every year just to keep growing

body.text: If the return on invested capital sits below the cost of capital, growth makes the problem bigger, not smaller. Indian telecom and aviation spent years growing subscribers and passengers while consuming capital. Jet Airways stopped flying in 2019 and Go First filed for insolvency in 2023. Both had grown for years before that.

children.text: Putting the Three Levers into One Formula

Valuation practitioners fold all three levers into a single expression. You will meet it again in Chapter 4, so read it slowly. NOPAT is operating profit after tax, g is the long-run growth rate, ROIC is the return on invested capital and WACC is the cost of capital.

body.caption: The value driver formula: growth, returns and the cost of capital in one line

children.text: Hold NOPAT at ₹100 crore, growth at 5% and the cost of capital at 12%, and change only the return on invested capital.

body.title: Value of the same ₹100 crore of profit at different returns on capital
Show me the arithmetic for the middle bar

children.text: NOPAT ₹100 crore, growth 5%, ROIC 20%, WACC 12%.
Reinvestment rate = 5% ÷ 20% = 0.25, so a quarter of profit goes back into the business
Cash left for investors = ₹100 crore × (1 - 0.25) = ₹75 crore
Value = ₹75 crore ÷ (12% - 5%) = ₹75 crore ÷ 0.07 = about ₹1,071 crore
Drop ROIC to 10% and half the profit must be reinvested, leaving ₹50 crore. Value falls to ₹50 crore ÷ 0.07, about ₹714 crore. Identical profit, identical growth, a third less value.

body.title: Turn the dial yourself
body.prompt: Using the same figures (NOPAT ₹100 crore, growth 5%, cost of capital 12%), what is the value if the return on invested capital is 25%? Answer in ₹ crore.
body.explanation: Reinvestment rate = 5 ÷ 25 = 20%, so ₹80 crore is left for investors. ₹80 crore ÷ 0.07 = about ₹1,143 crore. Notice that going from 10% to 20% ROIC added about ₹357 crore, while going from 20% to 25% added only about ₹72 crore. The first improvements in capital efficiency are worth far more than the last.

body.title: The expansion proposal
body.question: A business head proposes doubling capital spending in a division that earns 9% on invested capital. The company's cost of capital is 13%. The division's revenue and reported profit would both rise. What should the board conclude?
options: Approve it, because revenue and profit both grow
Approve it, because a larger division will command a higher multiple
Reject or restructure it, because growth at a return below the cost of capital destroys value
Defer the decision until margins improve, since margins are the only lever that matters
body.explanation: Every rupee invested at 9% when capital costs 13% loses 4 paise of value a year, and doubling the investment doubles the loss. Bigger reported profit is not the test. The test is whether the return clears the cost of capital. Fix the returns first, then grow.

children.text: Which Lever Should You Pull?

body.caption: Where each lever is won
headers: Who controls it day to day

cells: Better product mix, price discipline, cutting loss-making SKUs, renegotiating input contracts
Lower inventory days, faster collections, sensible supplier credit, sweating existing assets before buying new ones
New geographies, categories or channels, but only where returns clear the cost of capital

body.title: Twelve months to improve the valuation
body.scenario: You run a ₹400 crore revenue speciality chemicals business. The promoters intend to sell a minority stake in about 12 months and have asked you to improve the valuation. EBITDA margin is 12%, the cash conversion cycle is 110 days, and the plant runs at 65% utilisation.
body.prompt: What would you do, and what would you refuse to do?
body.modelAnswer:
What I would do:
1. Attack the 110 day cash conversion cycle. Every 10 days released is cash returned and a visibly better working capital story for the buyer. Collections discipline and slower-moving inventory are the first places to look.
2. Fill the idle 35% of plant capacity before spending anything on new capacity. Incremental volume on an existing asset improves both margin and return on capital, because fixed costs are already paid for.
3. Review the product mix and exit or reprice genuinely loss-making lines rather than cutting costs across the board.
4. Clean up the accounts early: separate related-party transactions, document normalisation adjustments, and get three years of audited statements consistent. A buyer discounts what it cannot verify.

What I would refuse to do:
1. Cut maintenance capital expenditure to flatter this year's cash flow. Diligence will find an ageing plant and the buyer will price the catch-up spending back in, usually at a worse rate than it would have cost us.
2. Stuff the channel with dispatches in the final quarter. It inflates revenue and receivables at exactly the moment the buyer looks hardest at receivables ageing.
3. Stretch suppliers beyond agreed terms to show a shorter cash cycle. It shows up in the payables ageing and damages supply relationships the buyer is paying for.
4. Chase revenue growth in a low-return segment purely to show a bigger top line.

body.title: The condition for value creation
body.textWithBlank: Growth creates value only when the return on invested capital is ___ than the cost of capital.
body.explanation: Below that line, every additional rupee invested subtracts value, and faster growth simply subtracts it faster.

body.title: Diagnose any business in six numbers
steps: Gross, EBITDA and net margin for the last three years, with the trend
The split of costs between fixed and variable, to judge operating leverage
Return on capital employed, and how it compares with the cost of capital
Cash conversion cycle in days, broken into inventory, receivables and payables
Revenue growth rate, and the capital that had to be invested to achieve it
Capacity utilisation, to see whether growth needs new assets or just better use of existing ones

body.label: Screener.in: Avenue Supermarts (DMart)
body.description: Open the ratios and balance sheet tabs. Compare the operating profit margin, ROCE and the working capital days with a branded goods company such as HUL, and notice how differently the two businesses make money.

cards.definition: The way fixed costs make profits move faster than revenue, in both directions.
Operating profit divided by capital employed. How hard the invested money works.
Return on invested capital, the after-tax version used alongside the cost of capital in valuation.
Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. How long cash stays locked up.
Growth divided by ROIC. The share of profit that must go back in to sustain that growth.
Growth funded at a return above the cost of capital. Any other growth destroys value.
Net operating profit after tax. Operating profit taxed as if the company had no debt.

points: Margins, capital efficiency and growth are the three levers behind every valuation number.
Margins are only meaningful against comparable businesses. DMart kept about 5.0% of revenue in FY25 and HUL about 16.6%, and both models work.
Operating leverage means high fixed cost businesses see profits swing far more than sales, a 20% revenue rise turning into an 80% EBITDA rise in this lesson's example.
Capital efficiency decides how much money is trapped to earn a given profit. Working capital days are usually the fastest lever a manager controls.
Growth needs reinvestment equal to g divided by ROIC. At 15% growth and 8% ROIC, a company must reinvest more than it earns.
Value rises with growth only when the return on invested capital exceeds the cost of capital. Below that, growing faster destroys value faster.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Sahyadri Services, Konkan Ceramics and the chemicals business are fictional. DMart and HUL figures are from published FY25 results, and the margins shown are calculated from those figures. Comparisons between the two are for illustration and are not a recommendation on either stock.
